game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Personally, I'm loving this game so far. I'll most likely update the review after the next three episodes come out, but I don't believe my opinions will change all that drastically.

Orwell is a game where you investigate a crime (a bombing, to be precise) using the brand-new Orwell system, presumably named after famous author George Orwell, author of 1984. Using the program, you can identify data that might be necessary to your investigation, slowly collecting it and linking it together to form a case for your superior to take a look at and give his verdict.

Some data is useless; do you really need to know what this woman's favourite colour or food is? Is someone's address being "somewhere over the rainbow" on one of their social networking profiles pertinent information to the case? No, and adding too much useless data can cloud the system, leading to the wrong conclusion by your supervisor at the end. One of my personal favourites was having someone logged in on someone else's account mention their profession, and it came up as data for the account's owner. Presumably, if in an online chat, you joked you killed a man, or were a descendant of King Arthur, that would show up in the Orwell system as important information.

Other data is in conflict; for example, if a Facebook timeline would have someone changing their relationship status to "in  a relationship with whoever", and then later changing it to "single", which one would be the correct data to input? You cannot remove data once you upload, so you have to think long and hard about which to use. Of course, in this example, you could look at whichever was more recent, but the decisions can be harder and more complicated than that, I promise you. I commend this game having pieces of in-conflict data show up as conflicted even if you haven't found the other data yet, so you can't choose A (the only option at the time) and then have option B, the secret correct answer, be revealed to you later.

You also have the ability to, once you have contact details (such as phone numbers, email addresses, etc.), access your target's phone calls, emails, chat histories. These play out in real time, but you can easily go back to searching through websites for info, and return once the conversation is done.

And I won't spoil anything, but the ending of the second episode had me almost falling off my seat in anticipation and anxiety, hoping my guesses weren't wrong. I punched the air and shouted "YES" pretty loudly when it was revealed I was correct. The game got me way more emotionally involved than I was expecting.

If the idea of this interests you, buy the game. It'll definitely be worth the money. If you're on the fence, never fear! There is a free demo which contains the first episode of five. You now have no reason not to go try it. Go try it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[i] *very, very minor spoilers are hidden* [/i]

[h1] TL;DR "The Last Enemy" without Cucumberpatch [/h1]

Admittedly, the above reference might skate over a few people's heads, but the core themes are the same. Based loosely around the old US Total Information Awareness system, the game explores the issues around predictive profiling and human bias.

The details are what makes this game shine: The irrelevant online junk, the typos and slang, the shoddy dating websites, even the pages load like a real browser. The user interface is slick and easy to use. For that extra immersion, I really recommend taking your time to read as much as you can. It's not as quirky as DX:HR, but it's close.

The characters are wonderfully complex, if occasionally stereotypical. I love the "show, don't tell" approach of implying their personalities through online interactions, and the format of the game is really unique -- I've never played a game quite like this before.

My biggest gripe is gameplay. There is none. Everything is highlighted and every conflict displayed, which underwhelms the idea that [spoiler] your bias invalidates Orwell [/spoiler], and eventually turns the game into a mindless point-and-click. There are no difficult puzzles or decisions beyond moral ones, and even those seem to have little bearing on the outcome. The ending certainly felt a little shoehorned, and the [spoiler] twist a little out of character [/spoiler]. It's best to view this game as an interactive story rather than a game. I'd have also liked the ability to replay individual episodes - restarting the game just to change a single decision in ep. 5 is a little inconvenient.

As a very fast reader, the entire game took 3-4 hours to complete, bearing in mind I read absolutely everything. Half the time seems to be spent on watching conversations scroll in real time, which is realistic, but not for the impatient. If you don't like reading or text-based games, don't bother.

I really do recommend this game. The tense, compelling plot had me eagerly waiting for the next episode. You do become emotionally involved with the characters, even with a week between episodes. A little shallow at times, but enjoyable nonetheless.

11/10 would hack the local fishing society again.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This is a difficult one to critique because whether or not you like it is mainly dependent on whether you like the narrative and how it is told. I’m not going to pretend that I know a huge amount about a good story well told, so when it comes to my thoughts on said story, take them with a grain of salt. Before I discuss that though, let’s talk about the game a bit.

[h1]“Interactive” Story[/h1]

In context, you are supposed to be a sort of investigator searching for clues about persons of interest via their emails, social media feeds, and phone conversations. I wouldn’t use the word “investigate” to describe the gameplay. Every import piece of information is already highlighted for you and you just need to drag-and-drop them to the appropriate location. When it comes selecting which documents you want to search through, there are indicators that tell which ones have important data-chunks. You don’t really have to read through the documents and phone texts unless you want story context.

This does streamline the gameplay experience, though. With a lot of story based adventure or point-and-click games, there is a risk of getting stuck at one part and losing all immersion in indirection proportion to mounting frustration. Orwell doesn’t have this problem as it is always very clear where you are supposed to look and this keeps a smooth pacing. As I mentioned earlier, this does contribute to the whole experience not feeling much like a traditional game as it feels much more like a guided tour of the characters and narrative progression. Perhaps a system where you have to highlight pieces of text you feel are important, and if you got the right piece then the story could progress? That may have been the original idea, but that could lead to many frustrations if you just barely missed the part of a quote you were supposed to get.

The only real gameplay in here is when there are two pieces of data that conflict with each other and you have to decide which one to submit to your superior. This could come in the form of two phone conversations by a character where one conversation makes him sound violent and the other makes him sound peaceful. Which one you submit will determine if that character gets arrested later in the story. This factors into a bit of a moral choice system regarding whether you try to paint the main characters and virtuous activists or terrorists. I feel an opportunity was missed to have more greatly divergent storylines to make the player feel like they have a real impact on the world. As it stands, your decisions only change minor events and what ending you get, with most of the heavy decision making existing in the last episode only.

[h1]Interactive “Story”[/h1]

With everything I’ve had to say about the gameplay thus far, you may be a bit perplexed as to why I recommend Orwell. Once again, this isn’t a typical [i]game[/i]. It’s a story with a bit more user control over the pace at which you progress through it. So how is the story?

Pretty good, actually.

The subject matter: government surveillance, is very topical and the game does a good job of showing the many different angles and opinions that people have about it. From those that try to peacefully discuss the issue, publicly criticize it, or are indifferent to it, every character seems believable and for the most part are consistent. The plot is revealed at a steady pace and is able to constantly engage. Appropriate music cues help to reinforce when something drastic has just taken place or when a particularly important piece of data is discovered and it does a good job of drawing you in. The last episode starts to deteriorate when the story starts to massively diverge and the amount of documents and computers to search through becomes overwhelming compared to the rest of the story.

While the data chunks are the most important piece of the story, there is a lot of text to sift through and it fleshes out the characters and game world quite well. A lot of it is unnecessary and for a while I thought that a small sub-plot about terrorism in another country was going to turn out to be a major plot device because the game kept bringing it up, but that ended up being nothing important. Also, documents and conversations are never deleted, so you are free to browse through them at your leisure and one small link could lead you down a rabbit’s hole worth of information. Having assessed these can be handy if the story calls for you to investigate those links and you’re already familiar with them, which does occasionally make you feel like a real investigator.

There are a few off moments when the characters don’t feel believable because we only see them communicate via text. Towards the end, [spoiler]everyone is panicking because they have discovered the Orwell system and can’t figure out how to deal with it,[/spoiler] and sometimes text just isn’t the best way to convey those sorts of emotions. These are hardly deal breakers though because what it boils down to is that whenever I would start the game up, it wasn’t because I felt some obligation to finish it. It was because I wanted to know what happens next. And no matter how many trivial nit-picks I have with the story, that single fact means I have to acknowledge that the story is engaging.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]

Orwell is a story, and not much of a game. Whatever gameplay is present serves entirely to incrementally progress you through the story and not present any kind of and challenge by itself. An experience like this lives and dies on whether or not its story is engaging which, to me at least, it certainly was.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b]My playtime:[/b] 10h (based on steam, 100% achievement; 2.5x playthrough)
[b]Grindy Achievement(s):[/b] No.
[b]Optional Achievement(s):[/b] Yes (17 achievements).
[b]Difficult Achievement(s):[/b] No.

[h1]Intro[/h1]
[i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] is a massive information gathering system where you, an investigator, is taking a role in sorting the relevant data and fix conflicting data that the system gathered to assist a crime. The game has story branching that persists over 5 chapters.

[b]Pros:[/b]
- 5 chapters
- Multiple endings and story branching that persists over the chapters
- Clean and fresh-looking interface
- You can restart a chapter after you finished the game

[b]Cons:[/b]
- Phone calls and chat animations take a very long time to finish
- Some clues are too hard to deduce unless if you know the full story
- You can't press the button to show conflicting data sometimes

[h1]Should you buy this game?[/h1]
[b]Yes.[/b]
[i]If you like to read or stalk people, you should buy this game. You also can buy it at a discount if you think that the playtime isn't worth the full price.[/i]

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[h1]In-Depth Review[/h1]

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
The interface is clean and fresh-looking. I like how the summary that is shown at the end of the chapter is introduced; it looks like the workboard in my office except that it's way cleaner.

As someone who likes to try something by doing it firsthand, I don't find the design to be confusing. The portal section looks like your regular website, the message section looks like your regular chat app, and the device section looks like the simpler version of your device.

I'm also impressed by how the dev showed the photos; it looks like a fragmented version of our faces and it looks so detailed even though it's not. The important facial like eyes and hair is shown although most details are blurred and fragmented.

The cutscene at the prologue skipped a few frames to me though, although I don't have any trouble in understanding the story because of that.

[h1]Story[/h1]
The story is being told by several conversations of your "adviser", someone who deduce things based on your findings, and whatever you read when you try to find clues, which are mostly from chat and phone calls.

Even though most conversations are held this way, I didn't find the main story to be confusing. Even if you couldn't understand the story, the "adviser" will give you some sort of info as to what is happening so you should be fine as long as you don't skip it. There's also a summary at the end of the chapter if you want to keep track of things.

There are several branchings in the game, either minor or major. I find the conversation between the branches to be smooth although some parts confused me since I didn't know the whole story at that moment. You need to play several playthroughs throughout the game to get all the major story branches and understand the whole story.

The thing is, there is no good or bad ending in this game; it's all about your opinion. You think what you think is good and bad. You also can deduce the whole story if you want or you can just understand the main story and be done with it.

[h1]The game[/h1]
[b]Features[/b]
There are 3 sections where you do most of your work: portal, message, and device. The in-game name is different, but I can't seem to recall the actual name since you don't need to know about the name to use it.

The portal consists of several web pages that you can access. The pages that you can access are limited to the system and more will show up as you unlock more clues.

The message, on the other hand, is a bit different. A message, either chat, email, or phone, will show up at certain times and you're allowed to wire-tap their chat and calls in real-time. The thing is, the chat speed is very slow. You can speed up the phone chat speed a bit although I still want it to be faster. It's taking too much time to listen to it especially when you're replaying your playthrough.

The device can be activated after you obtain a serial number of the target's device. You can access all files in the device, whether it's from a desktop or phone.

[b]Investigation[/b]
The suspect will have a profile page that you can fill with data. These data can be obtained by browsing through the 3 sections I mentioned. The data that you can take will be highlighted, either in blue or yellow.

Blue-colored means that there is no conflict with the data and yellow means that the data contradicts with other data. The game also has an option to show the conflicting data although I find that it's not working sometimes.

The thing is, you have freedom in choosing whatever you submit. I thought that I should fill all of the highlighted data in blue for complete profiling, but it's actually the opposite. All the data that you fill will be useful for the advisor's judgment and other people's fate, so you should decide carefully on what you submit.

Some data that you submit will change the story greatly, some are not. However, there are times where you have to make a major guess in determining the conflicting data that you must submit because you didn't know much and the clues are too vague at that point. Luckily, as I said before, there are no good and bad endings, so you can proceed as you please.

[b]Replayability and Length[/b]
As I said before, there are multiple endings. There are 5 chapters in total and each chapter except the last one lasts around 1 hour. I played the game fully twice and played one last playthrough from chapter 3 to unlock all of the major branching and achievement. It took me around 4 hours to finish all chapters at once.

Each chapter has a minimum of 2 endings that will affect the subsequent chapter. You can restart the whole story from the beginning or replay the chapter if you want after you finish the game once. Restarting the game from a specific chapter will delete all of the subsequent chapter data though.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
It's a nice game where you have to browse through things and wiretap people's communication to find out whatever is going on. The game has a lot of story branching and replayability.

review_text_raw:
[h1]The book 1984 by author George Orwell in a game. Splendid and intresting. While I've only read half of the book, I can still understand the connections. This must not happen in real life. I know it already does.. But we can still stop it..[/h1]
Ýou're yourself, a investigator with amazing spying tools. You get to spy on timelines, emails and even wire-tap phones.
You are looking for connections to put terrorists behind bars. The terrorists are bombing several buildings in Bonton, a fictional city in The Nation, a country where a Safety Bill has just gone through that puts investigators into control of the police work of The Nation. As a investigator for the law enforcement it is up to you to put the terrorists behind bars using Orwell. Orwell is a tool developed to find perpetrators before the crime is done. While there is flaws, terrorists and their groups are linked way faster than a human would think without the help of computers and social media sniffing.

[h1]This should remind us all of how NSA, FRA and GCHQ spies on us all today. No matter where we live in this damned world.[/h1]
Orwell is a scary game.. You never know what your state knows about you.. In some countries, people with odd political beliefs are put behind bars, freethinkers are disappearing and people who voted wrong are found and assaulted in their homes. While Orwell did not cover any of these points, it still covered the great amount of Internet hate you can get if you do anything wrong, even if it is just a single thing.

[h1]Pros:[/h1]

[list]
    [*]60+ FPS during the whole playthrough.
    [*]Think you're a NSA spy.
    [*]Very intresting.
[/list]

[h1]Cons:[/h1]

[list]
    [*]The game is far too short. I wanted to play more when I was to be arrested for knowing too much about Orwell..
    [*]It was buggy at times where I couldn't upload data until I restarted the game.
    [*]Nothing else.
[/list]

[h1]Ending notes of this quick review[/h1]
I am recommending this game to anyone, no matter age. This is a good game to learn from. Learn how the regime works. Learn how your country works. No matter if you live in a democracy or not there is always gonna be Big Brother spying on you. This game is more than just a simple game that only a fraction of people will buy. This game is a lifelesson worth getting. Nobody really cares how innocent you are. You are always a suspect when it comes  to state business.

I would like to thank the devs for 3 amazingly fun hours. It will be more because I am going for all the achievments!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Pros:
- The game brings awareness to important social problems: surveillance and totalitarianism
- Music is OK
- The characters are relatable
- Story is realistic
- This implementation of mass surveillance is plausible


Cons:
- Lack of depth in decision. The game is basically linear, except the ending which is a binary moral choice. No replay value.
- Lack of immersion stemming from weak game mechanics.
- The conflict system makes no sense and works against realisticity. How in the world can the system predict that something is in conflict with an unknown data chunk? A conflict should only be shown when both data chunks are known. 
- Phone calls wait for you to tap, such as everything in this game. No time pressure or feeling of urgency.
- The web is way too small, and computer hacking is way too minimalistic to be plausible.
- The enjoyment as you progress is almost a total downward slope. I think the last episode and the ending is just not ready.
- Game lasts no more than 8 hours.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I bought it after the RPS recommended it and... yeah it was one big disappointment... I didn't even finish it as it was so boring. The story is boring, the gameplay is boring, the graphics are eye hurting. Seriously if you are able to read quickly you will bore to death in this game. I was waiting for the texts to comin or for the calls to finish. As far as I can see the game is linear and there's an apparence of choice that is just an illusion. After the predictable ending of chapter 3 I said no more and uninstalled the game. 

Don't buy it. not even for the 3-4 hours of gameplay. I understand what the devs wanted to show - the ever present invigilation of govt in our lives and that taking things out of context can end very badly.Perhaps the problem is that I went in thinking this game would be like papers please - it's not. 

There is no game here at all, none. Instead, it's about dragging blue text onto peoples records, and then your supervisor, who speaks less with the tone of a long time bureaucrat that is spying on people, and more like a wet blanket that instantly talks with you extremely casually. Worst still, it makes government surveillance severely underpowered compared to reality.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The short review: I enjoyed playing this game, but I wouldn't recommend it. You should give it a try and form your own opinion though!

The long review: The game frustrated me because I expected a lot more narrative-wise since they used the name "Orwell". It definitely had parts where it excelled. The art is fantastic. The evidence gathering mechanic is a fun take on the traditional point and click genre. The story maintains a sense of mystery and suspense that can hook you in for the most part. Trying to figure out who Goldfels is and whether or not their intentions are truly malicious was what drove me to keep playing. I loved that there were also little easter eggs, such as a reference to "giraffes in hats" and articles about a 50 shades ripoff movie that made the game world feel more alive.

However, the writing... that's where this game falls short. There are other reviews talking about how the dialogue could be better etc., and I agree with them, but it wasn't the worst thing ever and it didn't ruin my experience. What DID ruin things for me was the game's last chapter. The narrative took a nosedive and the payoff completely ruined the setup. Most other reviews had no issue with the ending though, so you should definitely reserve your judgement and play the game first!


*****Some spoilers ahead*****

Just for context, I've only played this game once, and in my playthrough I prevented the 3rd bomb from exploding and decided to turn in evidence against Catherine Delacroix at the end.

The thing I hated MOST about this last chapter was the twist. Basically, one of the characters go "I was the person behind all those bombings bwahahaha". A real Reiner Braun moment.

This twist ending had two effects. First, it completely undermined the established mystery. Immediately, I felt stupid for caring about the game at all. What was the point of me working so hard then? Why did I collect all that evidence, if the criminal was just going to out themselves like that? 

The second effect was it made the whole narrative thematically unsatisfying. In the ending I received (I don't know if there are other possibilities), the criminal become the leader of the activist group with no repercussions. This was a person who'd set up two bombs that killed people. What pissed me off the most was that this person's friends acknowledges that this person committed murder, but based on the ending, it suggests all of them had decided to look the other way. Apparently, murder and thought manipulation is not a big deal when THEY are the ones doing it. So am I supposed to sympathise with this irresponsible group of people who have showed no regard for human life?? It's feels extremely hypocritical.

It really frustrated me because this game keeps telling me these people are innocent and I'm ruining their lives, but these people clearly aren't innocent. The worst things they did included: killing a police officer, doxxing a government agent, bombing and killing people at two separate locations, then attempting to cover up their crimes. Granted, some of these characters are more justified in their actions, but that doesn't change the fact that they actively ruined or tried to ruin people's lives. The only person I can say is mostly harmless in all of this is Themba. The game could've easily made this more nuanced by adding just one completely innocent character for the player to falsely incriminate. This one change would've easily revealed the flaws of the Orwell surveillance system, but that's not what happened. Instead, the game tries to guilt-trip you into feeling bad for outing people who have ACTUALLY done terrible things.

Maybe I only had a bad experience because my choices sucked. Maybe there is an ending where I get a better experience and justice is served to all, but then that implies there is a "right" way to choose, therefore you SHOULDN'T have the freedom to choose, your thoughts should be RESTRICTED so you choose only what the game thinks is right.

So what exactly is this game trying to tell me?

Orwell is hacking game inspiered on the life of the fantastic hacker Edward Snowden.
Basically you have to apply for a job as an investigator in a new highly security company that has installed cameras all over "THE NATION" to see if it dicreases the crimes per population so that they can expand the company for the others districts too. Anyways overall it is an excellent game , alovely one for ED´s fans...

review_text_raw:
[h1] DISCLAIMER: This is a full review, and NOT a first impressions review like all my other reviews, if you want a better full review, then please read better reviews then mine [/h1]

[quote] PLEASE NOTE: This review is being cast as a full review and not a first impressions review because the main bulk of the game is finished, although Orwell does have a story mode, it has different endings and choices, hence, this review is being cast as full because the main bulk of the game is complete, so please, think before you comment! Enjoy :) [/quote]

Orwell is a game developed by Osmotic Studios and published by Surpise Attack Games. Orwell is a compelling detective story that questions your morals, tugs your heart strings, and leaves you stunned. It has an intriguing plot that keeps you telling yourself "just one more episode..."

It does have some interesting characters who are easy to become attached to but not for long due to its short story and the game is intellectually satisfying. The game expects to absorb the world it has built and use deductive reasoning to back up your decisions and lines of investigation, basically meaning, it doesn't treat you like an idiot

However, Orwell is a fairly short game, finishing just one story with one ending in 2-3 hours is pretty damn short and currently there are no revising chapters and changing decisions. You have to create a new save from the beginning to pick different choices, however the developers have stated that they will change this in the near future with a patch

Orwell plays similar to a detective visual novel. If you are looking for flashy cutscenes and first/third person character control, then this is not the game for you. You are an intelligence agent working at your computer, and that is how you will experience this world. In my opinion, you do not need fancy graphics to appreciate the depth of this amazing story!

Orwell pays homage to one of the greatest writers of all time; George Orwell himself who has created some classic literary works such as Animal Farm and 1984 which this is inspired from!

[h1] RECOMMENDED :) [/h1]

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] Prelude:	[/h1]
For too long Telltale have had a vice grip on linear story-based games. Which is a shame considering only about 2 of their games were decent. So when I heard a new game had created enough favorable reviews and praise from people I trust, I decided to boot up: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You, or rather, Orwell: generic subtitle. 

[h1] Gameplay:	[/h1]
The game consists of reading through text, selecting infomation to upload to Orwell, a huge data base supposedly allowing to keep endless amounts of infomation on people (more on this later) you select outlined text or images, and choose wether or not to upload the data. Most of the infomation is required, but the game does a fairly decent job of shaking things up, infomation conflicting and choosing which one is most significant, the worst choice being: An online commenter calls guy A 'homosexual' meanwhile in a newspaper, it is stated he has been happily married with children. You choose which source is reliable. There also ends up being a data mechanic, only alloweed to upload 20 data chunks. The game does a [u] really [/u] good job of rewarding the player to go further, for instance near the end of the second chapter ([b] SPOILERS [/b]): [spoiler] There is a bomb detonating soon, with two people potentially offering locations of the bomb, if you dig deep into the email or messages (I think) of the people, you can see him admitting that he let his idea be pushed down, then using dates and timestamps, you can figure out this was just after the two people offered the locations. 	[/spoiler] This not only makes the player feel great after solving this puzzle, but also affects the endgame too. However the endgame is EASILY the weakest part of the game.

It is the [u] exact [/u] game issue as telltale games, maybe even worse. On the nose the character's tell you what you did, so averty it feels stupid. Not to mention.. [spoiler] The secret ending is locked off depending on how you handled a situation in Chapter 3, where you have to actively fail at your job to reach the good ending telling the police that a woman is armed and has knowledge of military which is FACT, you have to actively NOT tell the police this info, and THEN tell them her correct location, despite the fact the character says: 'I am not going down without a fight.' And you can accidentally trigger endings randomly, with supposedly 3/4 choices layed down right at the end, then wanting to do extra research, it doesn't say 'Are you sure, this will end?' Or something like that.	[/spoiler]

[h1] Graphics:	[/h1]
These devs are smart, at least in this department. The game is extremely stylised, meaning it will age very well. There was one time where I wasn't sure who was in a picture due to this, and it came as a suprise to me. Otherwise a few issues, there is no voice acting, even on phone calls. This shouldn't be an issue, considering other MAJOR review sites can get away with subtracting points from a game for having good voice acting rather than nothing. (yeah im still angry) If you also have Dyslexia maybe give this one a miss, it is a LOT of reading, and if you dislike the font, it doesn't change often enough to merit trying with this one.

[h1] Other:	[/h1]
The soundtrack starts off great, being the perfect sort of tracks for reading, not distracting enough to take you out of the game, but enough to stand on it's own. There is a few 'sting tracks' where they are used for shock, and this works mostly, apart from near the end where you are simply scrolling down and then you see some text and DUNNN, which was suprising and took the shock out of what I was reading because I didn't have to read it in time. It also starts getting REALLY repetitive near the end.

The game REALLY tries to be replayable, with the ability to skip to chapters 1-5, but a big problem are the phone calls, they average around 4.5 minuites in real time. With the final one, Chapter 5, where you would WANT to go through again first, too see if it could have ended different lasts around 10 minuites, of non-interactable text, which you would have read already. The game also isn't too long, if you read every article and looked indepth for everything I can imagine it lasting at around 5 hours, if you skip text and just look at the highlighted text, around 3 hours. For me, my playthrough was around 4.7 hours. A decent time, not too long, not too short.

[h1] TL:DR:	[/h1]
If you enjoy linear story-based games and want to see a good attempt or just a LINEAR STORY GAME WITHOUT TELLTALE IN IT, and enjoy reading, then its a recommendation, if you don't fit all 3 of those criteria, wait until a Steam Sale, or a Humble Bundle like I did. It does hint at some cool political ideas and ideologies, but that's more in the sequal.

Nevertheless, I look forward for the next Orwell game to go on sale and be fully out, I am a cautious fan, please keep up the good work devs, nice to see some varation in the gaming scene. You seem like cool guys too, patching stuff in and so forth.

-Thanks for reading
-Cain

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
A wonderful game.

Have you played a Telltale game recently? Do you notice that most of your decisions are cosmetic or mere distractions except for the one or two major decisions? You probably have thought about that. There are a number of different reactions to this fact. Either the games are so interesting you just don't notice/care (Walking Dead), you're willing to let it slide (The Wolf Among Us), or it absolutely spoils the game by making the player feel powerless (Game of Thrones).

What if there could be a game that took into account every decision the player made and changed the plot accordingly?

Orwell does this. In a way that is sometimes overwhelming.

The premise of the game is somewhat reminiscent of Papers, Please. You are hired as a government worker. Your job is to be connected to a massive spy-network which has access to the entire internet and can bypass all privacy settings. You're tasked with investigating a terrorist incident, finding suspects, and hopefully stopping their plans before they happen.

You cannot directly decide what or who to investigate. What you do is you highlight certain passages you uncover (from people's blogs, text messages, phone conversations, etc) and submit them to the system, which will then build its case in the direction the evidence will go. One of the first conflicts you're given to resolve is the investigation of a young woman who is a political activist. One who writes on her political essays "We are dedicated to peaceful means to promote political change," and then writes on her personal blog in a fit of anger: "DEATH TO ALL WHO DISAGREE WITH US!"

Do you submit the intellectual and rational example in an attempt to give the subject the benefit of the doubt, or do you decide the words spoken emotionally are her true feelings?

If you're getting the impression the game is meant to be a parable about the futility of massive surveilance and how invasive it is, there's one problem with that assessment: it's possible to actually succeed and prevent crimes this way.

The game gives the player a lot of credit in this respect. They don't settle for a straightforward storyline with a didactic message. There are certainly messages conveyed about surveillance and its implementation, how it affects people, etc., but the game's storyline is genuinely about the characters and the environment they're in, not a tract about politics.

If the gameplay sounds boring, be assured in that the game actually manages to make many scenes genuinely tense and thrilling as well. You will scramble to acquire more datachunks before time runs out and genuinely panic at some points.

It's a truly great experience, well worth the price, and I heartily recommend it because it really does make it feel like every choice you make, every little bit of data you feed to this huge system that guides the investigation really does matter.

Though there is one low point which I'll discuss. It involves some spoilers, so stop reading if you want to avoid them.


***spoilers***


The most conflicting thing about this game is its ending. Specifically there are three different types of endings with some variations between them. In this it's again similar to Papers, Please because the endings are either "Stay loyal to the government," "betray the government," or "do something else."

The problem is that none of these endings really... 'satisfy'.

With Papers, Please, all the endings were satisfying. If you stayed loyal to the government, you were congratulated for being a loyal citizen. You were able to keep your job. You were assured your life would continue and it would be good for your character. This is a very satisfying ending.

If you betrayed the government, you were also congratulated for doing so. You were given a vision of a new, better society you were helping to build and that you had genuinely done the right thing in helping the revolution. This is *also* a very satisfying ending. They both manage to be positive, even when the player does the exact opposite things. Perhaps it's not entirely rational, but a player who goes either path will enjoy their ending.

In Orwell though... none of the endings feel completely positive.

If you stay loyal to the government, if you prove the surveillance can work and bring down the terrorists and get the "ultra-loyal" ending, it leaves a bad taste in your mouth because you still don't feel like justice was done.

If you completely disobey the government, that doesn't feel right either. It doesn't feel like the people in opposing the government are right, or even doing things out of 'necessity'.

When I complete a video game, I want to feel some accomplishment. I'm fine with middling 'you did some bad things and good things, so you get a middling ending where both bad and good things happen,' but if I really put the time and effort to try to do everything 100% right by people, I want to feel congratulated with a positive feel-good "You did a good thing" ending. I want the game to acknowledge I tried. In that case, I didn't feel like there was enough celebration, so to speak. There's no 'ultra-happy ending'. Not necessarily a non-confrontational ending where no one is hurt, but at least one in which the guilty are punished and the innocent are spared.

The options that are presented for you to choose for your 'ending' are valid choices that I liked, but I think it could've used just a little bit more development to make it feel like a 'reward'. That is my only criticism, but even then, I replayed it through to see all the different variations, so it's not a game-ruiner by any means.

Again, it's recommended if you like story-oriented games with unique gameplay ideas.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I bought Orwell (on sale) expecting a sort of 1984 screens, eyes, with wiretaps everywhere. What I got was a message pop up game with a pretty compelling story. In that sentence, I just described the whole review. If you didn't get it - keep reading!

They say it's wrong to assume, and definitely after playing this, it's wrong to make assumptions sometimes. If there is a demo available, try it! This one didn't have it, and it was on sale - so I went for it. The [b]story[/b] is pretty good and well thought out, and has some serious twists and turns as it progresses. The characters are interesting and the game does a good job to keep the player guessing. The [b]gameplay[/b] revolves around making decisions on what to upload to "Orwell" (or the computer that connects all the dots) to decide the fate of the citizens that are being investigated. Basically. a text-rich game. Once a decision is made things get set in motion, very quick. During a specific period in the game I had the habit of uploading everything... just be careful what is deemed important! Someone may wrongly get arrested. 

The [b]visuals and graphics[/b] are very easy on the eyes. However, if you're someone who likes when the screen changes every once in a while, this might not totally be up your alley. The game consists of three or so main screens. The first is a headline type screen. This screen lets the player browse the web for interesting information they may come across. The second screen allows the player (working for Orwell) to listen in on live conversations or messages. The third screen is a computer hacking screen in which the player has access to a suspects computer. The game does a good progression to introducing the player to what is going on. The [b]sounds and music[/b] are pretty decent. There are moments in the game where the music will slam and something dramatic will happen. The sounds are alright and there is no live voice to the characters. I imagine being a small developper that can be hard to do, but the text does a decent job delivering a story. I'm not a text sort of gamer (my friend bought me Disco Elysium, I'm sure it's great, but just don't have the patience to play it), this game did catch my attention for a while though.

Why the negative review? If I had to warn my past self, I would advise my past self not to buy it. It's an awesome story, there are cool things that happen, but I feel indifferent to the game. I went down a mystery and I was put on the edge. Not enough for me to really like the game. If you like text based games and something that's a little different on Steam, or even mystery, decisions, and consequences... and especially if this game is on sale, I'd say definitely give it a shot. For me, I had a little fun. That's about it. It is sort of similar to Papers Please; Orwell is a little more linear to one story line. There are branches, but limited. The ending though, was definitely, as some would say, dope.  

This game has a story with a real lesson for the future. Would be interesting to see a new version of this game with more options and new tools to use.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] George Orwell rolls in his grave [/h1]

Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is an interactive novel exploring the increasingly popular notion that G. Orwell’s iconic “1984” ended up being a guideline for running a country, rather than a warning to its citizens. True to dystopian tones of its inspiration, the title opens up with a bombing attack on a public plaza. Several people were killed, perpetrators are unknown and public is in an uproar. This where you come in, as hand-picked investigator you will use the latest marvel of civil protection technology – Orwell, to solve the case. Orwell “the first and the last line of defence against terrorism” is a powerful software capable of accessing everything connected to the internet. Once a person is authorised by higher-ups for investigation, you are to upload any useful chunks of data into the software and Orwell will process them, granting you access to further information on the target. Person of interest has their phone number on their social media page? Now you can listen to their calls. An e-mail address published on their company’s website? Let’s take a peek inside. Is that a PC id number? You know the drill by now.

[b] Big brother stays vigilant [/b]
With power of Orwell at your fingertips, the player becomes breach of privacy incarnate, yet the decision whether to upload something or not is yours to make. At times you will have conflicting data, that may mislead the authorities acting upon your investigation, while certain details can be ignored altogether. On the other hand, there are also key data chunks that have to be uploaded in order to progress the story and, especially at early stages, there are not a lot of choices to make. Orwell is counterintuitive at first and software’s interpretation of data provided is downright puzzling at times. You better adapt to your new role quickly, as at certain junctions your choices will have an impact at the rest of the story.

It might have drawn your attention that I have addressed the title in question as an “interactive novel”, rather than a game. This is primarily due to the fact that aforementioned limited choice of data chunks thrown into the system is as far as gameplay goes. Alas, it is much easier to regard Orwell as a book, with webpages being equivalent of descriptions and eavesdropped calls and chats being the dialogues. Your investigation quickly unveils a hint of deeply-rooted conspiracy being at work and bombing is but a beginning of something much bigger. Plot divided into 5 chapters thickens quickly and while the general direction of the story is set in stone, your choices can greatly alter fate of certain characters and the ending is yours to twist.

[b] Blessed be the mind too small to question [/b]
Orwell is rather straight-forward with its thought-provoking intent. While the title’s plot unveils in delightfully ambiguous “The Nation”, it doesn’t take a particularly big leap of logic to start drawing parallels. Especially with themes of invigilation, media manipulation and a classic question of “whether the ends justify the means”. As with most of such questions and ideas, Orwell will be whatever you choose to make of it. It won’t be long though, as the title takes roughly 5 hours to complete, making it possible to finish Orwell in a single sitting. That said, the story is divided into coherent chapters of similar length, highlighted by the game as a good moment for a break, should you need one. Orwell is commendable for finding multiple sensible ways to underline impending conclusion of a plot thread, while staying reasonable from in-universe perspective.

Another facet of Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You, deserving a separate mention is the art style of the game. review_text_raw:
Conflict:  Orwell is an excellent game that is well designed and well written. 

Conflict: Orwell is a poorly written game that is horribly designed. 

Choose one. 

Orwell is a game that would demand someone choose one of these options, and the problem is is Orwell is an very good game, that is well written.  It however has some horrible design choices that stop me from calling it excellent or perfect.  In fact these design choices are VERY problematic. 


The entire game of Orwell is viewing webpages/conversations/phone calls and hunting down information and uploading it to a major database.  You're allowed free access to almost anything and you can upload almost anything to the database and play with it.  You'll get chastised for uploading garbage information, but it's also kind of fun.  Then the government who hired you to find the information will eventually operate on what you have found.   The story is told through these uploads and the results of your information gathering will change the story.  That's kind of cool. 

And Orwell tells a compelling (if a little predictable) story.  However it ends abruptly and seems to think it's ending can be a lot more impactful than it ends up being.   And then it falls into an egregious hole of pushing replayability but not allowing players to replay part of the story. 

But the thing is Orwell doesn’t really explain it’s gameplay.  The core of the gameplay is not what you upload, but rather what you choose not to upload, or how you choose to resolve conflicts.   But I really hate how it handles conflicts.  What it should do is allow you to upload conflicting information and have you choose how to resolve it explaining more “what do you think?”  Instead it makes this assumption that A or B is right and whichever you choose, they kind of operate on.  However that’s not how the world works, there’s conflicts in a single paragraph and the question is does the guy feel remorseful or does the guy feel responsible for the past… the answer is probably both, why make me choose. 

Then there’s other conflics that seem to not matter.  But what’s really important is what doesn’t get uploaded, and that’s kind of the problem. 

The first game you’re going to upload everything, because that’s what you think is right, but the game is VERY interesting when you don’t upload everything, you can change the game and the story minorly because of this.  You WILL end at the same point, but there is changes that happen. 

Sadly, the ending is a trinary Mass Effect style choice, that feels a bit eyerolling, even the “this ending is only unlocked if X” doesn’t happen and the end is really two or three screens.   I just want more interactivity in the story. 

The other problem is the final episode is actually excellent.  This is the episode where the game shines in a brand new way, it adds a new twist and limits the operator.  I almost wish this twist was added in day two or day three because it makes it much more intense to decide what you do, and I’d have liked to see the decisions on day 2 or 3 affect the ending, perhaps locking off the good ending if you fail. 

You see, the game feels a bit like the Teltale games, low interactivity, always reach the same ending and while that’s true, it’s not the same.  In Telltale, the same things happen no matter what, but in this game, there is changes, I just wish there was bigger meaningful changes that persisted, or even changed the ending and I’m hopeful for the future of Orwell because of that. 

But the story itself is good, if not as interactive as you like.  There’s good story twists, there’s good characters, and I actually like everyone involved in the story.  Orwell is supposed to be about the surveillance state, and even in that way Orwell shines.  And at 5 hours for a full gameplay it might seem expensive, but it can easily be played a second time.  

However replayability does suck, almost the entire game is the same and you have to play at least 3 or 4 hours to replay it.  I wish each episode would be replayable separate so I could go get the three endings of episode 3 and 5 without the full replay.  I didn’t mind a second replay but the third is abusive.

Overall though I DO like Orwell, the litmus test for this game is “did I put season 2 on my wish list” and I did.  I liked it that much.  10 bucks seems high but I think it’s worth the money, and even if not you can get it on sale.  It’s a unique experience, and a fun and interesting take on the surveillance state.  But even my complaint about the design and the way the game really presents it’s gameplay doesn’t ruin and interesting and engaging story. 

I’m hopeful, I want to see season 2 have more interactivity, I want to see season 2 involve more limitations on the user, and I want season 2 to be better, but for a first season of a rather novel game type, I’m pretty happy.  Orwell delivers what it intends to and I do adore how it does so.

review_text_raw: Orwell fails on a lot of levels. A lot of very fundamental writing levels. First and foremost it gives you a set of tools that allow you to see what people do on the internet and tasks you with finding the perpetrator of a bombing. You're given one prime suspect and as you progress your web of people of interest grows and grows. The principle gameplay mechanic involves choosing which specific pieces of information you choose to report to your orwellian system. Which will change how the game plays out. The first failure comes that it is often very obvious what information is going to affect what, as it is all highlighted in blue, or yellow if it conflicts with another piece of information. This is another problem. The conflict system makes very little sense most of the time. One of the first examples of the system in use involves a personal blog ran by a Person of Interest and an editorial they wrote for a newspaper. They both detail the same concept but with completely differeing opinions on the matter, and these pieces of information are considered a conflict and therefore cannot both be reported. While this specific instance makes very little gameplay difference either way it still makes no sense. Being able to report both pieces of information would have shown (at least to me) his willingness to play whatever side of an issue would get him paid, and could've sowed him as a much stronger suspect later on. Instead you have instances where you handler is confused by information you weren't able to provide them due to it being a conflict, when both pieces of information were true. This creates a very frustrating experience in trying to influence the story and with trying to keep information that is relevant to the story seperate from information that isnt. Another fundamental failing of the story telling is its ending, which if I'm perfectly honest; is godawful. To my knowledge, your choices throughout the game have no impact on the ending. There's just three buttons at the end. Push one for your ending. None of them making  a bit of sense. Right before your ending the perpetrator of the bombings reveals themselves, showing that the previous three chapters had all just been misdirection to make sure no player could possibly guess the real one and they basically say to you the player "And this is why your system doesn't work! You couldn't even figure out I was the perpetrator" When it was the game mechanics and information that was provided to you by the game that made it impossible to determine the perpetrator. They then ask you to take down the system, since you can now see it doesnt work. your other two options are to get a politician associated with your orwell system arrested, or to claim the group the perpetrator belongs to are all terrorists using out of context IMs. If you're thinking that this seems to be lacking a very obvious fourth option then I agree. My first instinct was simply to use the perpetrator admitting to instigating the bombings to get her arrested. As that would make sense, she admitted it to our face and yet there's no option present. Just the three arbitrary ones presented. In the end it was three chapters of intriguing build up for one chapter of letdowns and unguessable twists that completely kill the narrative, suspension of disbelief, and immersion. 4/10

review_text_raw:
The Game is best described as an interactive crime novel rather than a full game.

[Pros]
It is well designed and the interaction is very streamlined and has a nice flow to it, combining the feeling of going through files like an actual investigator without the boring drawback of having 500 duds for every lead. IMO the devs nailed the ratio of work/reward in a way that is engaging, story driving and entangling.

The plot is interesting and apparently it has multiple endings with yet again multiple outcomes, it is by no means a "choose your own adventure" but it brings in just enough individuality that a second and even thrid run of the game could be interesting even if you already know the plot.

There are always multiple ways to get them juicy Data chunks you're looking for.

[Cons]

The game does a pretty good job at highlighting important information, be it in form of Data Chunks or in plain text. However oftentimes you find yourself in a spot where you discover information about a person you know has some sort of realationship with one of your POIs. However the game does not let you add said information to their profile which to me came as an enormous break in the flow.  As in: "This person seems to play a pivotal role and I have information about them that might come in handy later, why in the lords name am I not allowed to add this information?" [spoiler] Although this has happened to me a few times I most often encountered this with the lawyer, Joseph if im not mistaken, he is an important character early on yet the game does not let you collect data on him from the get go [/spoiler]
To me it felt like the game does not reward you if you are being extra thorough, which can be very discouraging.

Maybe I have not been thorough enough, but the game has major plotholes, the most annoying to me being the algorythm of Orwell knowing two data chunks are conflictive. How does the programm know that? And if it found such intricate information out without me going over it why am I needed? This could have been solved much more elegantly by having to chose which of the two statements is true; As in "her favourite colour appears to be red but in a previous statement we have assest that it is indeed blue. Do you wish to edit your previous assesment or keep the original?". This could have also gven us more opportunity to bond with our evaluator, whom I have perceived as rather robotic since he basically only shows emotions when you make mistakes. [spoiler] Honestly the big J plottwist was such an anticlimactic ending, although I understand her "motivations" I do not understand how harrison fits in the picture. The life insurance was for his mother ofc. But did he also fake correspondance as Abraham? How does that fit in? Why did we not find any indication of this earlier? It felt like a very cheap reveal alà modern sherlock holmes, where the pieces just happen to fall in a way nobody could have predicted and resolving the story in a very dry and undercut way. How did they manage to find out initiate's number? Why dont we have access to that if they can just, hypothetically, recall? [/spoiler] This way of resolving the main plot does not do their way of engaging storytelling justice in the slightest. 

[Verdict]

A very different approach to the interactive novel, I enjoyed it altough it has some shorcomings. The way the game involves the player and tells it's story is superb and deserves a better plot than what we are given.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I've always been one to read all of the books/letters/e-mails in games, but they rarely do more than build the world or give character backstory. I also tend to agonize over decisions in dialogue trees, worried that the "wrong" answer will cut me off from more interesting story lines. Orwell is a game that completely commits to reading and interpreting as the primary game mechanics. It succeeds at telling a satisfying story, even if it sometimes trips on the complexities of these mechanics as storytelling tools.

There are issues: The interface isn't as robust as you would hope. For instance, you can drag pictures of people from the Web into their profile, but only certain ones. At one point I found pictures of two new "persons of interest" on their corporation's website, but I couldn't drag their photos into their profiles. The game also runs into the issue that we have expectations of what can be done on the Internet. For instance, when you get the ability to break into someone's phone and can see where they've been, you expect that the addresses will tell you what is actually at those locations, but Orwell doesn't tell you this, you have to either remember or infer what is there.  

You can also get trapped when the story tries to funnel you to a certain plot point. In one part of the game there was nothing for me to do but to choose between two pieces of conflicting information: Which of two people organized a protest? The problem is that there was no way for me to make that call, it was pure he said/she said. I had a hunch, but it wasn't backed by any concrete information, and given what I had come to realize was the black-and-white nature of the Orwell system, I wanted to have something concrete before making this decision. Unfortunately, in order to progress the story I was forced to make the call based on nothing more than a hunch. 

And sometimes it seems like you need to make the wrong choice when one set of conflicting information would clearly open up a whole new tangent and the conflicting data wouldn't, so you choose the first even though you know the second is just as likely to be correct. For instance, at one point a character was accused of being gay, but there was conflicting information that he actually had a wife and kids. Of course, these two things don't conflict at all, there are plenty of gay people who have been in heterosexual relationships and even marriages. In fact, this character left his wife and children and the accusation that he was gay came many years later, so clearly one could argue that he left his wife and family BECAUSE he was gay. But in order to progress the story and open up profiles on the wife and learn more about that part of his life, I had to choose the wife data over the gay data. 

Sometimes the AI just breaks, especially that of your handler, Symes. For instance, one time I added the info that a certain character had a new girlfriend, that he wasn't with his old girlfriend, Juliet. Symes chimed in that he never knew that this character and Juliet were a couple, but I had put that information in both of their profiles a long time ago. And sometimes Symes is just clueless: At one point we discovered the name of a new character, one for whom we previously only knew her online handles, and he said something like "So she's been hiding her real name, eh?" Of course she was! Who always uses their real name for their online accounts?

It seems that there are probably multiple endings, but I only played it through once. There are no manual saves, so to get other endings you would have to play through the whole game again, which I'm not interested in doing. I wasn't entirely satisfied with my ending, but I still think that the journey was compelling and timely, probably more timely than the developers even realized when they started working on it. Orwell is a fascinating experience, especially if you are at all interested in our current information culture and the balance between government data gathering and personal privacy.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
An ultimately disappointing game. It's very short (~3 hours for a full run even if you are taking your time and reading everything), which I can forgive if the game is excellent but it's not.

The gameplay itself, as others have noted, is drag-and-drop pre-highlighted bits of text. Some of this text is mandatory for the game to proceed, some of it is optional. It's not always clear which, so it's easy to get stuck if you are doing a replay and want to see what happens if you ignore bits of evidence, and you may accidentially find yourself doing the same thing that you did last time.

A lot of the choices you make (up until episode 5) are relatively inconsequential, you'll get different text but the overall plot remains the same. Unfortunately there's no way to replay an episode to see what would happen if you did something else; supposedly this feature is being worked on, but in a choice-driven game this should have been a feature that shipped; Tell Tale has had this feature since The Walking Dead season 1.

I thought this game was going to be more about the surveillance state ala 1984, Person of Interest, etc. but I wouldn't say this is a good critique. True, you are reading other people's emails, but we're not investigating some political dissidents who said bad things about Great Leader, we're investigating an actual in-universe violent incident (and someone who potentially wants to commit more of these.) So while snooping through the emails of the suspects, it's not unreasonable to think that you are trying to catch people who legitimately committed a real crime. The game does try to railroad you a bit to force you to investigate someone who may not be the offender, which you can ignore, but this is pretty late in the game.

Some of the story beats just don't work; for instance, in the final parts of episode 4, [spoiler]information about your handler is leaked and the game forces you to drag-drop some of his personal information into his file. There's zero reason to actually do this, it's only to force the user to involve someone who clearly isn't a related to the crimes. And that would work if it was optional, but it's not. It's a "you are meant to feel bad right now" bit, and just falls flat.[/spoiler]

The "good ending" is pretty trash, [spoiler]everyone sings the freedom song and topples down statues and gives you a plaque for spilling the beans, ask Snowden how that's working out for him. It's rather corny.[/spoiler]

Overall had decent potential and the demo (episode 1) is pretty good, but fails in the end stretch.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is an narrative game with unique gameplay. The game puts you in the shoes of an investigator whose job it is to keep the Nation safe. You work with the titular program 'Orwell' which is an advanced search engine that lets you browse the in game internet in search of terrorists. You will start of by reading through public blogs, forums and social media. But as the stakes rise and the public information dries up you will find yourself spending more and more time eavesdropping on phone calls and hacking into personal files.

The feel of the game reminds me a bit of Deus Ex. I personally loved hacking computers and reading emails in those games, and Orwell turns this side activity into a full game. This means that you will do a lot of reading, although the useable pieces of information are always highlighted. You can upload these 'data chunks' to your superior, who will act on the information you feed him. Your superior cannot read anything except for the parts you upload, which gives you the freedom to interpret the data and even 'spin' it. Do you focus on the information that marks someone as potentially dangerous or do you focus on their peaceful side? This will ofcourse have consequences down the road.

Speaking of consequences, these are actually real in this game. Although your actions will not change the core structure of the narrative, they will have a very clear impact. All suspects can be arrested, one can be killed, or you can let them all go free. What makes this game unique is that most consequences are not directly tied to a single choice, but to a whole set of smaller decisions. There is no 'do you let this person live?' moment. Instead the choices you made in what data you upload and what information you ignore will determine the fate of the characters. The ending may appear to be a 'choose your own ending' affair at first, but a replay made it clear to me that your earlier choices will still impact the ending you get.

The theme of the game is privacy vs safety. But unlike other games or media on this subject, there is no clear black or white. The game shows that your work can save lives, but that it also has the potential to ruin them. The characters constantly move between light grey and dark grey, sometimes praising violence and sometimes worrying about their family. Only in the final episode do two characters clearly turn out to be evil, but even then the game takes no position on the core debate, allowing the player the freedom to think about it themselves.

Sadly the game has a very short runtime. The first play through will take about 4-5 hours. If you skip past most text you will be done even faster. The game has some replay value, partially due to its short length, but the first play through is much more fun than the second.

There is one potential problem with this game: it is all in text. If you like reading lore, this will be fine. But if you tend to skip across text, the game will likely become boring fast. Even the phone calls are in text. Only the intro is animated. Despite this, the game can still be nail biting tense as police move in on the potential location of a bomb or terrorist and you can do little but follow the news and related phone calls, hoping that your work was enough to save the day.

Tl;dr: a great narrative game with actual choices, but lots of text. If you skipped to the tl;dr there is probably too much text for you!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
It's alright, I wrote a pile of text giving my detailed opinions on the game when steam graciously changed pages to warn me of an update and trashed my entire progress... I don't have the patience to write it again so here goes the short version with the important tidbits:

[list]
    [*] Orwell is a Visual Novel that tries to give a new coat of paint to the genre, kinda like Analogue a Hate Story. You read the plot through logs while doing your "job" of uncovering the truth. Props to the originality. Art style and UI is great and unique.
    [*] For a game that clearly takes upon George Orwell's work, it's not thought-provoking enough. It's very one-sided and not well written enough to make you really care. The only really Orwellian characteristic of this game is that the ending will thoroughly let you angry. It's not a bad thing given that the books 1984 and Animal Farm do just that, the real problem is that this alone can't give you a good experience when the ride there wasn't meaningful enough. The political thriller portion of Orwell is very stereotypical.
    [*] The detective portion of the game is great. If the game were focused solely on that with the political drama in the background, it could've been an amazing experience.
    [*] Decisions are very, [i]very[/i] poorly implemented. They don't change anything in the big picture and the branching path is the laziest type possible of a negative-sum game. You'll always see one side losing because the characters always act as stupidly as possible. To give a couple examples without spoiling anything, you have one witness that has an crucial information to prevent a disaster, and you can only get it out by blackmailing and ruining that person's life, keep in mind that by then you [i]know[/i] that person is innocent. The investigator assigned to help you is probably the most inexperienced and innefective cop ever seen when it can not even get a simple non-invasive information of someone who would cooperate if asked and not threatened. You'd argue that maybe this was the main critique of the game, but it was poorly implemented, it wasn't well written enough to make you believe such an absurd situation could ever happen. The same thing happens later when warning of an armed suspect prompts the investigator to give a "shoot ot kill" order when everything you have on the suspect is still circumstantial. Orders like "shoot to kill" are not so lightly given, especially not to law enforcement. Keep in mind that Orwell is NOT 1984, it's not the same envinronment and not the same setting, Orwell is closer to our reality than 1984's one.
    [*] For a game with so little branching paths, it's very short. 4 hours to finish it while playing leisurely
    [*] The dev clearly did not account for replayability. There's no option to skip dialogue or fasten the pace of the game. You can choose a chapter and that's all, choosing an earlier chapter will also void subsequent ones.
[/list]

That's basically it, you might think I have more bad things to say than good, that's something I adressed in my full review prior. Short version is: Given the price tag and the positive experiences throughout the game, I don't think it warrants to not reccommend because of that. I do want, however, that people know the game's shortcoming before buying. Most of these do not bother me and I'd probably still buy the game if I knew before playing, but some people wouldn't.

review_text_raw:
what a SUPERB game!!

I started it just to try it out and give it a go (I got it in the monthly humble) but I found myself so much attached to it I had to finish it all in two sessions!

The game plays out like a detective game, it feels mostly passive because the only thing you can do except reading the events is to gather infos and try to make them as much reliable as possible to the context. the "choice matters" is absolutely present, but at the same time it's not clear when it happens, which is good. no more "the character will remember that" (you hear me telltale??).

There are two things though I disliked. First, what you gather is mostly final, especially with conflicting chunks. I understand what they're doing here, by forcing you to investigate on your own properly before giving out an answer, but sometimes data is ambivalent (one character thinks something, another the opposite with no factual truth in between but just speculation on how you see it) or just ambiguous. Then, when it's uploaded, it's done. Other times you upload things and your advisor jumps to conclusions or take the information literally or completely out of context, some other times they give a background to it. It's very inconsistent and it made me feel "will it understand correctly the meaning of this upload?"

Second, - I will keep it spoiler free - and this one has been a big one for me, there's no neutral ending. At least none that I could find. You can either be the gov's dog by forging evidence, or the rebellious revolutionary that destroyed the system. No in-between. 
This will probably trigger somebody, but I found Orwell a decent tool for investigations, while the whole game continuously point at it as inherently bad, so if you support it you must be bad. I think no tools are good or bad, it's how we use them and we can see it in this game the ethical modifications done to it have improved it by far. It has flaws, true, (especially if you give the tool to an untrained person treating it as a game... what the heck, seriously.) but all in all if the system is actually restricted to investigate actual threats it could be an interesting way to manage it. We all had to deal with terrorists lately unfortunately, and we all cry for help and for prevention. This might be another tool to help us. 

So I don't get why you HAVE to be bad if you support it? Why can't you just incriminate the bombers and call it a day? why do you need to fabricate evidence or else being called disobedient and incriminate yourself? Very bummed by this choice in the climax of the ending.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] "For The Nation, for the security of the citizens, for their safety, I shall be the investigator. The one who shall observe and... eliminate." [/h1]

What is in this mysterious name: Orwell? A good plot? Realism and coherence? A branching storyline? Memorable characters? Plot twists? Perhaps, all of the mentioned and a lot more? Yes - all of the mentioned and A LOT more. This game is a very interesting game in which you'll act as an investigator working for a governmental project called "Orwell." With the help of this mass surveillance software/tool, you will be tracking and evaluating various people to identify potential "threats" to The Nation. The evaluation process includes analyzing social media accounts of the people evaluated, their chat histories, emails, phone calls, personal devices, and etc. Basically anything, which they deemed a part of their "private" life. 

What I really liked about this game is its attention to detail. On the first look, the game's storyline contains lots of unnecessary snippets of information, which might be regarded as useless by the inattentive player. However, those little details and discrepancies form a larger picture which reveals a major plot twist that takes place somewhere in the ending episodes. The plot twist itself [spoiler], which was about Juliet being the imposter instead of the suspected Harrison,[/spoiler]did make sense after some other playthroughs (accomplishing all the achievements and endings) as I've paid a lot of attention to those little details in the game. [spoiler]For me, the hint provided by Symes about Juliet's favorite book (The Mockingbird)and Harrison's lost phone seemed like the ones which can directly lead you towards the "Juliet is the true imposter" conclusion. [/spoiler]Well, the game proved to me that no story can be regarded as completely explored without the consideration of all the small details. A lesson well learnt.

As much as I liked this game, there are still things that can be improved. For instance, adding a setting for an accelerated playthrough, because DAMN, some of the calls take more than 10 minutes to finish and are unskippable. Going through the game again becomes a real pain without this feature. I understand that some events happen during phone calls (which is probably why you can't accelerate them), but as a person who finished the main plot multiple times, I don't bother to read all the stuff again. Besides, I think players decide beforehand their choices, so adding the accelerated playthrough won't hurt the experience much (it is wise to lock it until the game is completed for the first time). There were some spelling (Episode 3; objective; "motiviation") and grammar mistakes, but those are minor issues. Apart from these, there aren't much things which I'd want to be added to this game. 

I've written too much for this review already and thus will conclude my overall impression for the game. The game is truly amazing BUT is not for everyone. If you crave for action and excitement and don't like reading and analyzing, then I do not recommend this game to you. But hey! It's never a bad time to explore a new frontier and discover a little bit more about yourself. Maybe you'll love this game the same as I did and give it a thumbs up. 

[u]-QG7 Recommended[/u]
